one_line_contribution: An item-level placement law for distilled agent experience: a label-free statistic — the fraction of *deployment* queries for which an item would enter top-k ("coverage breadth") — decides whether that item belongs in the always-on instruction or the retrieval bank, and the payoff of promotion is claimed to be the top-k slot it vacates rather than the promoted text itself.
closest_prior_work: Two threats, one conceded and one not. (a) Conceded: working-set estimation and frequency-based cache admission. The proposal's own Related Work admits that "estimate future access from a deployment-representative window rather than stale logs" is working-set estimation, and that MemGPT/A-MEM instantiate the usage-frequency version in LLM agents; running MemGPT-style promotion as arm E2(v) caps the damage but also caps the contribution. (b) Not conceded, and more damaging: the paper's claimed *inversion* — "promotion is valuable because it vacates a slot in the competitive tier, a benefit with no analogue in caching" — is false as stated. Exclusive cache hierarchies (victim caches, exclusive L2/L3) are defined by the property that promotion into the fast tier removes the block from the slow tier and frees its capacity, and that is exactly why they are used. Separately, admission policies built around cache pollution and scan resistance (LRU-K, LIRS, ARC, TinyLFU/W-TinyLFU) exist precisely because high-frequency or high-recency items crowd out items that would have served other requests, and their standard remedy is to *refuse admission* to polluting items — i.e. the crowding-out mechanism this paper presents as new is the textbook motivation for admission control. Once the inversion argument fails, the remaining differences the proposal lists (accuracy rather than hit rate, content/framing change on promotion, always-full tier) are real but are differences of setting, not of claim, and the surviving novelty is "we measured a known allocation principle in an LLM-agent memory bank." That is a workshop-sized delta unless the empirical results are unusually clean. Third, in dense-retrieval terms breadth is hubness: because each calibration query admits exactly k items, Σ_m b(m) = k identically, so "broad" items are just the embedding-space hubs of the query distribution, and hubness correction (Radovanović et al.) and MMR-style diversification are prior art on the same phenomenon.
strongest_objection: The mechanism claim contradicts the measured result the track brief tells the proposer to treat as the starting position, and the proposal misreads that result as support. The pilot found that *injection volume* was the causal lever: cutting seven retrieved items to three eliminated the harm from the same bank, with topically correct retrievals. Slot competition predicts the opposite sign of the same intervention. E3 stakes the entire mechanism on P3, "hybrid-with-refill beats hybrid-without-refill by ≥3 EM points at k=2" — that is, adding back a lower-ranked, more marginal item helps. The pilot says adding items hurts. No-refill at k=2 is literally the volume reduction (k=2→1) that the pilot's 7→3 result says should be the *better* arm. If the pilot generalizes, P3 comes out backwards and the paper's own refutation clause fires ("the benefit is token savings, not slot competition"). Worse, the matched-token constraint in E2 means the hybrid cannot win by volume reduction either: the consolidated block is present on every episode and the freed slots are refilled, so total injected experience per episode is held roughly constant by construction, while the pilot says total injected experience is the only lever that moved anything. Under a straightforward reading of the prior results, the modal outcome of E2 is that breadth hybrid ≈ pure top-k ≈ MemGPT promotion at matched tokens, all within the 2.5-point indistinguishability band, and P2/P3/P4 all resolve to "placement does not matter once tokens are matched." Second-order but also serious: E1, the "core test," has an effective sample size of 14 for the tested quantity. Four item-level fixed effects (b, u, f, length) on 14 items leaves ~9 residual df; the 150 queries per item and the query random intercept inflate nothing for an item-level slope. And the 75/75 stratification of the 150 queries into m∈top-k and m∉top-k equalizes exposure across items by construction, which is the very thing breadth is supposed to vary — A(m) measured on an exposure-equalized set is not the placement advantage that obtains in deployment, and the stratification mechanically attenuates the breadth coefficient the paper needs to be positive.
what_would_fix_it: Three changes, in priority order. (1) Reconcile with the pilot before running anything: add the volume-monotonicity curve (accuracy vs. k at k=1,2,3,4 with a fixed bank) as E0(c) and state, pre-registered, what P3's refill-beats-no-refill prediction implies given that curve's slope. If accuracy is decreasing in k in this setup, the refill prediction is already refuted and the design must change; if it is flat or increasing, the pilot's volume result does not transfer and the proposal should say so up front rather than citing volume harm as confirmation of slot competition. (2) Turn the dialed-in skew into a law. P4's effect size is a free parameter: the authors choose the Zipfian skew of the history stream, so "breadth beats frequency by ≥3 points" measures the knob, not the world. Sweep the skew (report effect size against KL(history‖deployment) at three or four levels, reusing the same bank) so the claim becomes a dose-response relation rather than a single manufactured contrast; this also subsumes the unskewed positive control at no extra design cost. (3) Fix E1's estimand and power: drop the 75/75 stratification in favour of sampling queries i.i.d. from the deployment distribution (so exposure varies with breadth as it does in deployment), and raise the item count from 14 to ~40 at n=60 each — the same 4,800-episode envelope buys 2,400 more effective df on the only coefficient the paper calls its core test. Separately, either uncap the MIPROv2 arm or drop it: a 400-rollout MIPROv2 on a 7B is a strawman and losing to it would be uninformative, while beating it proves nothing.
missing_baseline: A de-hubbed / diversified fixed-k retriever at the same k and the same token budget — the retrieval-side fix for exactly the phenomenon the paper attributes to placement. Concretely: (a) MMR or DPP-diversified top-k, and (b) a hubness-corrected score (CSLS, or per-item mean-similarity subtraction / query-side centering) computed from the same 500 unlabeled calibration queries breadth already uses, so it costs zero extra labels and zero extra episodes. This is the baseline a reviewer will demand because the identity Σ_m b(m) = k makes "high breadth" and "embedding hub" the same property: if simply preventing hubs from monopolizing top-k recovers the hybrid's gain, then nothing was learned about instruction-vs-bank placement, the entire consolidation apparatus is unnecessary, and the finding reduces to "dense retrieval over a small memory bank has a hubness problem." Drop-only (E3c) does not cover this — it deletes broad items outright, whereas de-hubbing keeps them retrievable for the queries they genuinely fit, which is the strictly better policy the paper never tests. A distant second omission: MemGPT-style promotion computed on the *calibration* stream rather than the skewed history, which would isolate "fresh data" from "coverage statistic" and reveal whether P4's win is anything more than the conceded working-set-estimation principle.
preprint_collision: The check is not thin — it is empty, and the proposal says so: the search tool failed on every invocation, zero titles were retrieved, and the closest-work list is explicitly recollection. The honesty is creditable and the pre-committed withdrawal clause is more than most submissions offer, but under this track's own standard an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness, not a neutral, and this is the second or third round in which it has gone unfixed. Judged on content: the decision problem is already occupied by MemGPT's core/archival paging and A-MEM's consolidation, which the proposal concedes and now runs as arm E2(v); the statistic is occupied at the level of principle by working-set estimation, also conceded; and the "inversion" that is supposed to survive both concessions is contradicted by exclusive cache hierarchies and by pollution-aware admission control (TinyLFU/LIRS/ARC), which the check does not consider. That leaves the collision surface larger than the proposal's own assessment admits. On live preprints, the most likely scoop is in the agentic-context-engineering / playbook lineage the proposal already cites: ACE-style "grow-and-refine" curation with de-duplication and merging of repeatedly-useful bullets into a persistent context is one step from "consolidate the items that keep getting retrieved into the always-on block," and context-budget-allocation and hot/cold memory-tiering preprints in the Mem0/Letta/ReasoningBank orbit are exactly the natural next paper. I cannot name a specific title with confidence and will not invent one — but that is precisely the burden the submitters have to discharge and have not, so I score novelty as unestablished rather than absent. The stated commitment to a dated search log is the right remedy and should be executed before, not after, the experiments are run, since a collision would redirect which of E1/E3/E6/E8 becomes the paper.
